messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 44

# The Weight of Footsteps

Marcus is twenty-five years old and works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in the city. He is soft-spoken and methodical in his work, someone who takes quiet pride in leaving a room exactly right. He has held this job for two years and, by most outward measures, is managing. But the life Marcus carries inside him tells a different story.

Growing up in a small town in rural Ontario, Marcus was raised primarily by his stepfather after his mother began working long shifts at a processing plant. From around age seven until he left the house at seventeen, Marcus was subjected to regular physical beatings at the hands of this man — a volatile, unpredictable figure who could shift from calm to explosive without warning. The violence was rarely precipitated by anything Marcus could identify. A chair scraping the floor, a meal going cold, a look misread — any of these could end with Marcus pinned against a wall or knocked to the ground. He learned to read the house the way some children read books. The sound of a truck in the driveway. The particular weight of footsteps on the stairs. Whether a beer had been opened. He became an expert in anticipating danger, and that expertise never fully left him.

He moved out at seventeen, couch-surfed through his late teens, and eventually found stable footing through the hotel job. He is good at the work. The routine of it — the carts, the folded towels, the sequence of tasks — gives his days a structure he finds genuinely comforting. But the job also places him in circumstances that his nervous system cannot always distinguish from the past.

When a guest raises their voice in a hallway, Marcus feels his body go rigid before his mind has registered anything. His heart hammers. His hands stop working. He describes it as "going somewhere else" — a few seconds where he is no longer in a hotel corridor but somewhere smaller and more dangerous. He has learned to find a linen closet, close the door, and breathe until it passes. His coworkers think he is simply private. They do not know what is happening inside those closets.

At home, Marcus sleeps poorly. He keeps his apartment sparsely furnished and meticulously clean — a habit he cannot fully explain but that feels necessary, like maintaining control over at least one environment. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, sometimes from a dream he cannot remember, sometimes from no dream at all, just a sudden and absolute certainty that something is wrong. He checks the locks. He checks them again. He sits on the edge of his bed and waits for his body to believe it is safe.

He has largely withdrawn from social life. He had a small group of friends from a previous job but has let those connections thin out. Dating feels impossible to him — not because he doesn't want closeness, but because the vulnerability it requires feels genuinely threatening. He describes himself as "not good at being around people for too long," though what he means, and what he is beginning to slowly understand, is that intimacy activates something in him that he has spent his entire life trying to keep quiet.

What strikes Marcus most about his current life is not the nightmares or the startle responses or the sleeplessness — it is the exhaustion. He is tired in a way that rest does not fix. He has been vigilant for so long, scanning rooms and reading silences and preparing for impact, that he no longer knows what it would feel like to simply exist without that hum of readiness underneath everything. He is twenty-five years old and he cannot remember a time when his body felt like somewhere he was allowed to rest.

He came to therapy, he says, because he is tired of being tired. He sits with his hands folded in his lap and speaks carefully, as though choosing each word for its safety.
